cards.headline: Profit is a magnet for competitors.
cards.body: A business earns fat margins. Rivals notice, copy the product, and cut prices to win the customers. Margins fall back toward average. That is the default ending for most profitable ideas — unless something is defending them.

cards.headline: A moat is a structural defence.
cards.body: Picture a castle. The walls are the profitable business; the moat is the ditch that makes attacking expensive. In a company the ditch is not effort or talent. It is a feature a rival cannot copy just by spending more.
Moats come in four shapes. Each is a different reason a customer stays put or a rival stalls at the edge.

cards.headline: Two of them work on the customer.
cards.body: Switching costs: moving your payroll system to a rival means retraining every manager, so you stay even when a cheaper option appears. Network effects: a payment network is worth joining because everyone else already joined, and each new member makes leaving worse.

cards.prompt: Which is more likely to keep a rival out for a decade?
cards.explanation: Talent can be hired away; a licence cannot. **Cost advantage** works the same way — a rival can copy your process, but not the scale or the location that makes each unit cheaper to produce.

cards.title: Margins with no defence
cards.caption: Nothing holds the rivals back, so they copy the product and undercut on price. A moat is what would have kept this line flat instead.

cards.body: A moat shows up in the numbers as margins and returns that stay high for years instead of [[1]].
cards.explanation: One strong year proves nothing. Durability is the test: profits that survive a decade of other people trying to take them.

cards.headline: Moats get filled in.
cards.body: A patent expires. A regulator opens the market. New technology makes an old switching cost irrelevant. So the question is never only whether a moat exists. It is how fast it is being worn down, and by what.

cards.summary: A moat is the structural reason a profitable business stays profitable while everyone else tries to take the profit.
bullets: Competition drags high profits back toward average.
Moats come from intangibles, switching costs, networks, or cost.
Durable margins and returns are the evidence, not the story.
Technology and regulation can fill a moat in.

cards.insight: Anyone can earn high profits for a year. The question worth asking is what stops someone else from taking them next year.
